articles.title: 376 yards, and Fortree ran out of field
articles.dek: Accel BeckhmJr caught three touchdowns, Dram Marino accounted for seven, and Mossdeep reached 12–0 with a 79–13 victory.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Accel BeckhmJr needed eight catches to produce 376 yards at Fortree. One went for seventy-seven without reaching the end zone. Another covered seventy-five and did. The distinction mattered for approximately one snap, because Shawn Mareman finished the first drive from a yard out. Fortree spent the afternoon discovering that a successful pursuit could still leave Mossdeep an extremely short trip to the next touchdown.

The Eclipse won 79–13, improved to 12–0 and added another extraordinary receiving performance to a season already crowded with them. Dram Marino completed twenty-two of twenty-six throws for 550 yards and four touchdowns, then scored three more times on the ground. BeckhmJr caught three of the passing scores. Mossdeep led 38–13 at halftime and outscored the Skyhawks 41–0 afterward, turning a comfortable lead into a result that will follow both teams well beyond this week.

That second-half shutout deserves room beside the passing numbers. Fortree had found two touchdowns in the second quarter, including a fifty-five-yard Floatzel run. The Skyhawks then went the rest of the game without another point. Derrat Brooks finished with five sacks and sixteen pressures; Armaldo Pace added the sixth sack. Rabsca completed fifteen of thirty-nine for 167 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions. Mossdeep's offense kept shortening the distance to its next score while its defense kept increasing the difficulty of Fortree's next possession.
The first long catch left one yard

Mossdeep's opening touchdown drive began with ordinary gains. Mareman ran for six. Ninjulio Jones caught passes for eleven and fourteen. Gronkaludon added nine, Jones supplied another thirteen, and Marino scored from a yard out with 3:59 left in the first quarter. That sequence is useful context for everything that followed: the Eclipse could sustain a possession before the spectacular throws began arriving.

The next touchdown possession required only two plays. At 2:22, Marino found BeckhmJr deep left for seventy-seven yards. Mareman ran right for the remaining yard at 1:56. Fortree had kept the receiver out of the end zone and still conceded seven points. A defense can take pride in the chase; it would generally prefer to avoid making the chase its principal contribution.

Mossdeep's third scoring drive crossed the quarter break. Jones ran for seven, Mareman gained seven, and Poury Holt supplied three before losing a yard. On third-and-eight, Marino found Gronkaludon for nine. The tight end added thirteen on the first play of the second quarter, and Mareman ran up the middle for an eleven-yard touchdown at 5:41. The lead reached twenty-one points after the extra point. Two distinct receiving threats and several runners had already contributed.

Fortree finally answered through Floatzel. The back gained fifty-five yards on a third-and-three run to the right at 4:37, ending a five-play touchdown drive. It was the sort of explosive response a home crowd needs when an afternoon has started badly. Mossdeep responded even faster. On its next offensive snap, Marino threw deep right to BeckhmJr for a seventy-five-yard touchdown. The play began at 4:24; the receiver had restored the separation before Fortree could turn its own long run into a sustained recovery.

body.alt: Dram Marino, a Drampa in Mossdeep number 12, releases a pass.
body.caption: Dram Marino threw for 550 yards and four touchdowns, then scored three times on the ground.

body.text: The last competitive stretch

The Eclipse still made mistakes. A second-quarter fumble gave Fortree another possession, and the Skyhawks used it. Brooks sacked Rabsca twice on the resulting drive, yet the passer found enough completions to continue, including a third-and-twelve conversion to Floatzel. Rabsca eventually hit Dudunsparce for a twenty-six-yard touchdown at 1:37. That made the score 28–13 before the unsuccessful extra point.

Fortree's satisfaction lasted through the kickoff. Jones returned it for a touchdown, giving Mossdeep an immediate answer without requiring Marino to take the field. The first-half scoring ended with Adam Vinathorn's twenty-three-yard field goal. The Eclipse had produced touchdowns through passing, rushing and a return, then added a kick. Fortree had enough successful plays to explain its thirteen points and too many unsuccessful sequences to keep those points within reach.

The halftime score also helps separate this game from a single spectacular receiving total. BeckhmJr supplied the largest gains, but Jones had scored on special teams, Mareman had finished two drives and Marino had already scored on the ground. Gronkaludon's conversions kept earlier possessions alive. When Fortree stopped one player short, another had repeatedly finished the work.
Four catches that removed the remaining doubt

BeckhmJr opened the second half with catches of forty-one and twenty-four yards on consecutive plays, the second for a touchdown at 5:33. The two-play possession covered sixty-five yards. After a Fortree punt, he caught another deep throw for forty-five, then a short pass for thirteen. Marino ran in the remaining yard. In two possessions, four catches had produced 123 yards and helped Mossdeep score twice.

The next touchdown took eight plays. Mareman carried four times at the start, Gronkaludon caught an eight-yard pass, Holt ran for six and BeckhmJr added thirty through the air. Marino finished from one yard again. That third rushing touchdown explains the quarterback's unusual final ground line: four carries, two yards, three scores. It was an afternoon of very large passing gains and very small remaining distances.

Fortree forced another fumble early in the fourth quarter, and Mossdeep punted once later in that period. Those interruptions belong in the account. A 79-point result can make every possession sound inevitable, but the recorded game includes wasted chances and useful defensive plays. The problem for Fortree was the number of possessions on which its successes did not carry over to the next series.

BeckhmJr's final touchdown came on a seventy-one-yard pass at 3:58 of the fourth. Gronkaludon later caught a three-yard scoring pass, and Mareman completed the scoring with a five-yard run. BeckhmJr finished with eight receptions on eleven targets. Gronkaludon caught eight of nine for ninety-five yards and a touchdown; Jones caught all four of his targets for fifty-two. Mareman added seventy-three rushing yards and three touchdowns on fourteen carries.

body.alt: Derrat Brooks, a Raticate in Mossdeep number 54, prepares to rush.
body.caption: Derrat Brooks supplied five of Mossdeep’s six sacks.

body.text: Voices after the game

“I thought seventy-seven was a perfectly good distance,” BeckhmJr said. “Apparently Shawn wanted the last yard. Very considerate of him to keep me from doing everything.” The receiver’s grin suited an afternoon when eight catches had given Fortree considerably more running to do than it wanted. Mareman’s finish also made the joke accurate: the long reception needed another snap, and the back supplied it.

Marino was more measured. “The protection gave us time, and the receivers finished the throws,” he said. “The long gains were there today. We still had to make the right decision on the next play.” That distinction becomes useful against Petalburg. Mossdeep can carry its timing and execution into the next game; it cannot assume the same spaces will appear.

Michael Dorrill pointed to the defense’s response after halftime. “They hit us for two scores in the second quarter. We kept working and gave them nothing after that,” he said. The six sacks and two interceptions give that assessment substance. With defensive absences accumulating, the Eclipse will need another coordinated effort against a much more accurate passing opponent.
Petalburg brings a different test

Mossdeep's protection gave Marino room to produce those numbers. Fortree recorded no sacks. Tyran Armstead and Bastony Boseli each had eight pancakes in the box score, while the offense finished with 646 total yards. Those figures support a broad account of offensive control. They do not require assigning every long completion to a particular blocking matchup that the record does not establish.

The injury report adds a less celebratory consequence. Luvrelle Revis is now listed out two weeks after the Fortree game. Ninjaskamara remains out three, Richard Furman four and Marshall Flock two. Revis had an interception and two forced fumbles in this win; losing him changes the available defensive personnel even after a dominant result. Michael Dorrill has a fresh availability problem to address before Petalburg arrives.

The Pride are 9–3 after beating Dewford 14–10. Mossdeep has already secured Hoenn East, but the remaining schedule includes Petalburg, Canalave and Sunyshore before the final two division games. Those opponents provide immediate reasons to keep examining protection, replacement roles and defensive consistency. Fortree's two second-quarter touchdowns remain useful review material even when placed beside a sixty-six-point margin.

For the Skyhawks, now 3–9, Rustboro visits next. Floatzel's seventy-three rushing yards and Dudunsparce's touchdown offer concrete plays to build on. Rabsca's six sacks and the defense's 550 passing yards allowed identify much more substantial work. The home crowd saw several impressive individual efforts. Mossdeep turned its own into eleven touchdowns, and Fortree never found a way to make the next long throw difficult enough.

art.alt: A wide view of Fortree’s forest-canopy stadium during the Mossdeep game.

articles.title: Saffron gives Vermilion no second escape
articles.dek: NeMarcus Tare made four sacks, Jolt Train Ln returned a punt for a touchdown, and the Psi Corps won the rematch 34–0.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Vermilion had already shown how to beat Saffron by one point. Saffron answered the rematch by allowing none. The Psi Corps won 34–0, improved to 10–2 and left the Volts with a much less comfortable account of their season series. The earlier 10–9 result remains in the standings. It will require considerably less space in next week's conversation.

NeMarcus Tare recorded all four Saffron sacks and fourteen pressures. Jolt Train Ln returned a punt seventy yards for a touchdown. Dam Skattebo ran for ninety-three yards and a score, while HeeDee Lamb caught seven passes for 126 yards and another. Archam Manning threw two touchdowns despite completing only sixteen of thirty-eight attempts. Saffron had enough ways to score that an uneven passing day did not become a competitive game.

The defense has now allowed three points across its last three games: 52–0 against Fortree, 35–3 at Cinnabar and this shutout. Those results total 121–3. Trent Scarboro's club has allowed seventy-three points all season, and Vermilion contributed none to that total here. The practical achievement goes beyond making a familiar opponent uncomfortable. Saffron has repeatedly kept its offense from needing an excellent performance on every possession.
A return changed the margin

The first quarter produced only an Octillery field goal, though the distance made it memorable. The fifty-nine-yard kick at 4:13 put Saffron ahead 3–0. Vermilion survived the rest of the period without allowing another score. At that stage, a low-scoring game still suited a visitor whose earlier win in the matchup had required only ten points.

The separation arrived through the return game. Shiinotic punted fifty yards to the Saffron thirty with 5:15 left in the second quarter. Jolt Train Ln returned it seventy yards for a touchdown. Octillery added the extra point, and the lead became 10–0. Vermilion had completed a defensive stand without escaping the consequences of surrendering the ball.

That sequence is central to the result because it supplied a touchdown without asking Manning to solve the coverage. The quarterback's final completion rate leaves room for criticism, and the Volts' secondary did make plays. Meganium intercepted a pass and recorded six pass defenses; Tentacruel added five. The punt return gave Saffron a different answer while the passing offense was still working through those problems.

Manning found Gengar Pickens for an eight-yard touchdown with 1:32 left in the half. The extra point made it 17–0. Saffron had moved from a three-point lead to three scores of separation through one return and one offensive touchdown. Vermilion entered halftime needing both better finishing and a way to prevent the game from continuing on those terms.

body.alt: Jolt Train Ln, a Jolteon in Saffron number 9, carries the ball along the sideline.
body.caption: Jolt Train Ln’s punt-return touchdown added special-teams points to Saffron’s shutout.

body.text: Tare kept the passing game expensive

Chandelure completed twenty of forty-two passes for 198 yards. He threw no interceptions, which matters when assessing the defeat: Vermilion's passing problems did not come from repeatedly handing the ball directly to a defensive back. The Volts struggled to convert completions into points and gave up four sacks, all to Tare. Forty-two attempts produced fewer than two hundred yards and no touchdowns.

Victreebel supplied the largest receiving contribution, catching two passes for sixty-six yards, including a forty-six-yard gain. Galvantula added thirty-seven on three catches. Kangaskhan caught six passes but gained only twenty yards through the air. That distribution explains why the completion count alone gives an incomplete account of the offense. Several successful throws created very little distance toward the end zone.

The ground game offered limited relief. Kangaskhan rushed twelve times for thirty-four yards, Wigglytuff added twelve on five carries and Chandelure gained one. Vermilion finished with forty-seven rushing yards. A run of eighteen accounted for more than half of Kangaskhan's total; the remaining attempts did not provide a dependable way to keep the offense ahead of its next passing down.

Saffron's defense also spread the supporting work around Tare. Furfrou recorded eight tackles, Pach Tatum five, and Swampert four. Watchog had six pass defenses and recovered a fumble. Demedicus Ware finished without a sack but recorded five pressures. Tare owns the headline number; the rest of the unit supplied enough stops and contested throws to make that number useful throughout the game.
The fourth quarter still offered a warning

Octillery's fifty-two-yard field goal at 1:37 of the third quarter pushed the lead to 20–0. The next scoring change did not arrive immediately. Early in the fourth, Vermilion completed a short pass to Ariados, who fumbled after a nineteen-yard gain. Watchog recovered for Saffron. On the following offensive snap, Manning's deep pass was intercepted by Meganium and returned twenty-two yards.

The exchange is worth retaining in a comfortable victory. Saffron's defense created a possession, and the offense immediately returned it. The Volts failed to turn that opportunity into points, but the sequence gives Scarboro a specific item for review. The final score does not turn an interception into a useful decision, and future opponents may punish the same mistake more effectively.

Skattebo made the next decisive contribution. His twenty-seven-yard touchdown run up the middle at 2:43 increased Saffron's advantage to 26–0 before the extra point. The back finished with sixteen carries for ninety-three yards, averaging 5.8. L'oudre Swift supplied twenty-two more yards on six carries, while Pickens gained eleven on three. Saffron's 126 rushing yards gave the offense a productive alternative to its lower-percentage passing possessions.

Lamb completed the scoring with a twenty-six-yard touchdown catch on third-and-four at 2:00. His seven receptions accounted for 126 of Manning's 205 passing yards. Mothel Irving added fifty on four catches, and Pickens had thirteen on two, including the earlier touchdown. Lamb was the principal downfield source, but Saffron still found a second scoring receiver when the available distance was shorter.

body.alt: HeeDee Lamb, a Heliolisk in Saffron number 11, rests with an American football.
body.caption: HeeDee Lamb finished with 126 receiving yards.

body.text: Voices after the game

“The rush worked together,” Tare said. “I got the sacks, but there were other people making the quarterback stay where I could reach him.” It was a characteristically modest description of a four-sack day. Saffron’s coverage and pressure had complementary jobs, and the final passing line shows how little Vermilion received from either its short attempts or its efforts to escape downfield.

Skattebo was equally quick to share the credit. “The line kept giving us something to work with,” he said. “You want to reward that, especially when the defense is getting everybody back on the field.” His contribution mattered to the shape of the game even when the most conspicuous points came through the air and on the punt return.

Trent Scarboro welcomed the shutout while retaining an offensive assignment for the week ahead. “We finished enough drives to separate. We can still be more consistent between those finishes,” he said. Sixteen completions in thirty-eight attempts leave room for that improvement. Saffron can celebrate a convincing division victory and still bring a specific passing problem into practice before Viridian arrives.
The division lead grows

Vermilion fell to 7–5, three games behind Saffron. That gap gives the Psi Corps a much stronger position than the narrow first meeting suggested, although the season series itself is now split. The Volts remain in the current playoff field. Their record still represents seven wins, even as a minus-sixty-three point differential documents how severe some of the defeats have become.

For Lt. Surge, Pewter's visit provides the next chance to restore offensive production. The Rockers just lost 13–3 to Celadon. Vermilion cannot assume another small scoring total will be sufficient simply because that approach has worked before. It has scored seven and zero in its last two games, and Saffron showed how quickly a close-game formula becomes irrelevant when the opponent supplies points on special teams.

Saffron hosts Viridian next. The Titans surrendered a 21–0 halftime lead to Cinnabar in a 29–21 loss, giving Scarboro another opponent with fresh evidence of offensive opportunity and costly mistakes. The Psi Corps can reasonably expect their defense to create difficult possessions. The offense's task is to make better use of those possessions than sixteen completions in thirty-eight attempts might ordinarily permit.

Three straight dominant defensive results have put Saffron in position to pursue more than a place in the field. The remaining work includes the division and conference seeding, with Mt. Silver and Blackthorn still ahead in the current seed order. Tare's four sacks, Train Ln's return and Lamb's late touchdown gave the Psi Corps another win toward that work. Vermilion left with the earlier victory intact and a much clearer view of the distance it must close.

art.alt: NeMarcus Tare, a Ninetales in Saffron number 42, leaves the field.

articles.title: Mt. Silver secures Johto West with 45 unanswered
articles.dek: Garshawn Lynch ran for three touchdowns as the Reds shut out Olivine and clinched their division at 11–1.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Mt. Silver returned from its first defeat and secured a division championship in the next game. The Reds beat Olivine 45–0, reached 11–1 and completed the head-to-head sweep that settled Johto West. Garshawn Lynch ran for 131 yards and three touchdowns. Tic Thorpe threw three more. The defense gave the home crowd an entire afternoon without an opposing score to interrupt the celebration.

The clinch follows a precise route. Olivine is now 6–6 with five games left and can reach eleven wins. Mt. Silver already has eleven and owns both meetings, including the earlier 13–9 victory. The other division clubs cannot reach the Reds' current win total. Connor McLarren's team has secured Johto West and a playoff berth, with five regular-season games still available to improve its postseason position.

That accomplishment came one week after Blackthorn ended the unbeaten run with a 30–22 victory. The Reds could not reverse that result here, but they could show a better response than a week of explanations. They rushed for 188 yards, received an efficient passing performance from Thorpe and turned Olivine's mistakes into repeated scoring chances. The game was 28–0 by halftime.
The first turnover became seven

Olivine's opening opportunity ended when Quilladin fumbled after a four-yard reception at 4:33 of the first quarter. Mt. Silver's Ninjask recovered. Thorpe subsequently found Sceptile for a five-yard touchdown with 3:05 left in the period. The Reds had converted the visitor's first major mistake into the lead.

The opening score established a pattern that became much more expensive in the second quarter. Olivine could complete passes, but a completion did not always end with possession safely retained. Drampa finished twenty-one of twenty-nine for 136 yards. That is a high proportion of completed attempts with modest total distance, and the fumbles made some of those successful throws actively damaging.

Lynch scored his first touchdown on an eleven-yard run up the middle at 2:50 of the second quarter. On Olivine's next offensive snap, Drampa completed a fourteen-yard pass to Beedrill, who fumbled. Machamp recovered for the Reds. Lynch finished the ensuing opportunity from a yard out at 1:41, again running up the middle.

The Ironclads then surrendered the ball through the air. Drampa's deep-left pass at 1:34 was intercepted by Tauros and returned nine yards. Thorpe found Plusico Buress for a six-yard touchdown with thirty seconds remaining in the half. Mt. Silver had scored three second-quarter touchdowns, and the last two followed turnovers that prevented Olivine from mounting a sustained response.
Lynch restored the running threat

body.alt: Tic Thorpe, a Togekiss in Mt. Silver number 42, reaches for a pass.
body.caption: Tic Thorpe gave Mt. Silver another productive way to move the ball.

body.text: The previous week's defeat had included only thirty-seven Mt. Silver rushing yards. Lynch alone supplied more than three times that total against Olivine. His twenty carries produced 131 yards and three scores, with a longest run of sixteen. The result came through repeated useful gains and finishes, rather than one extraordinary run accounting for most of the afternoon's production.

Vibrava added forty-nine yards on seven carries, averaging seven yards per attempt. Thorpe gained eight on two runs. Together, the three runners gave Mt. Silver 188 rushing yards. The passing game therefore did not need to account for every first down or every scoring opportunity, and Olivine could not treat an incomplete pass as the beginning of an automatic escape.

Lynch's third touchdown came on a twelve-yard run at 2:46 of the third quarter. Like his first two, it went up the middle. The repeated direction is a recorded feature of the scoring plays; it does not identify a single defeated blocker or a specific defensive call. What it does establish is that Mt. Silver finished three separate opportunities through the same broad area of the field.

Lynch remains listed with a minor injury entry carrying zero weeks on the new report. That designation should be read as reported, without inventing a diagnosis or promising a future workload. His 131 yards and three touchdowns are confirmed production from this game. His availability for the next one should continue to follow the actual team report.
Thorpe kept the passing game economical

Thorpe completed eighteen of twenty-two passes for 188 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. He took one sack. His day complemented the rushing production because the incompletions were infrequent and the scoring opportunities were finished. A team already controlling the ground game has little reason to apologize for a passing total that matches it almost exactly.

Gregar Jenings caught all four of his targets for sixty-three yards. Plusico Buress caught five of six for thirty-nine, and Doduo added a twenty-seven-yard reception on his only target. Jenings supplied the final passing touchdown, a twenty-five-yard catch deep right with 3:23 left in the fourth quarter. Thorpe had already found Sceptile and Buress for the first-half scores.

The spread of recipients matters when considering the Reds' response to Blackthorn. This game did not require a single receiver to carry an enormous share of the offense. Lynch repeatedly finished on the ground, the passing touchdowns went to three targets, and the defense created possessions. McLarren received contributions from several parts of the roster before the result became a rout.

Venusaur added a forty-six-yard field goal with thirty-nine seconds remaining. That completed the scoring at 45–0. The final kick was a small part of the result, but it also completed a second half in which Mt. Silver added seventeen points while Olivine remained scoreless. The Reds continued producing after the division-clinching outcome had become increasingly likely on the field.
Olivine's completions went too little distance

Magmar led the Ironclads with thirty-eight receiving yards on four catches. Tranquill added twenty-three on three. Gastrodon caught five passes for fifteen yards. Those are useful details for understanding why Drampa's twenty-one completions did not produce points: many ended close to where the play began, and the offense never found a scoring pass to offset the lost possessions.

body.alt: Garshawn Lynch rests on Mt. Silver’s bench after the victory.
body.caption: Garshawn Lynch’s 131 rushing yards and three scores helped secure Johto West.

body.text: Gabite rushed nine times for thirty-seven yards, with Vibrava, Tranquill and Growlithe adding twenty-four between them. Olivine finished with sixty-one rushing yards and 197 total yards. Mt. Silver's corresponding total was 376. The Reds did not need an overwhelming sack count to control the game; one sack, one interception and two recovered fumbles were enough when paired with restricted gains and their own scoring efficiency.

Olivine is still part of the wild-card race at 6–6 and currently holds the final Kanto–Johto place. Its next trip is to Blackthorn, now 10–2 after winning at Violet. Jasmine has an immediate reason to address ball security and the distance gained on completed passes. A second difficult road opponent offers little time to recover the opportunities lost here.
Voices after the game

“Everybody got to enjoy that one,” Lynch said. “The blocks were there, the catches were there, and the defense kept handing us another turn.” The back’s enthusiasm was earned across three scoring runs. Mt. Silver had spent the previous week discussing a loss; a division-clinching shutout gave the entire sideline a much happier subject.

Thorpe offered a shorter assessment. “Clean catches. Useful yards. Keep the drive moving,” he said. His receiving work gave the Reds another way to advance while Lynch handled the rushing touchdowns. That balance matters against the remaining schedule, particularly when Saffron arrives next week with a defense that has allowed three points across its last three games.

Connor McLarren treated the title as an achievement worth marking. “They earned the division over the whole season. Today they finished the job,” he said. The next job is protecting the conference lead. Mt. Silver can enjoy a banner without confusing it with a bye, and the coming sequence against Mahogany, Saffron and Cinnabar will supply plenty of reasons to keep preparing.
The remaining prize is seeding

Mt. Silver visits Mahogany next with the division secured and the conference lead still worth protecting. Blackthorn and Saffron are both 10–2, one game behind. Winning Johto West guarantees entry to the postseason; it does not guarantee the conference's first-round bye. The distinction gives the remaining schedule a clear purpose after an afternoon that settled the first objective.

Josh Alakazam remains listed out nine weeks, so the Reds continue to work with their available personnel rather than an assumed immediate return. Thorpe's efficient game and Lynch's restored rushing production are concrete reasons for confidence in that group. They also provide a standard to carry into the next matchup, where the previous week's success will not count toward the score.

The home crowd received the result it could reasonably have wanted after Blackthorn: a decisive win, no opposing points and a confirmed division title. McLarren can now prepare for Mahogany knowing that the postseason place is secure. The next five games will determine how favorable that place becomes and how consistently Mt. Silver can reproduce the complete performance it delivered against Olivine.

art.alt: Garshawn Lynch, a Garchomp in Mt. Silver number 22, celebrates the division title.

articles.title: Seven touchdown passes, five takeaways, one runaway quarter
articles.dek: DeZhaun Watzon and Jolt Vick finished the chances Sunyshore’s defense supplied in a 53–17 win at Hearthome.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Sunyshore scored twenty-seven points in the third quarter at Hearthome. The Starseekers entered halftime ahead 20–3 and began the fourth ahead 47–3, having repeatedly turned a defensive takeaway into a short route to another touchdown. DeZhaun Watzon finished with seven passing scores. Jolt Vick caught three. A game that had remained within reach early became a 53–17 Sunyshore victory.

The Starseekers improved to 9–3 and retained the Sinnoh East lead. Their offense gained 342 yards, only seven more than Hearthome, but the teams used their possessions very differently. The Haunts threw three interceptions and lost two fumbles. Sunyshore threw no interceptions and received seven touchdown passes from twenty completions. Field position and finishing explain the large scoring gap more clearly than the small difference in total yards.

Watzon completed twenty of thirty-one for 227 yards and took no sacks. Fera LaGatr caught ten passes for ninety-six yards and a touchdown. Vick caught four for eighty-nine and three scores. FLOAT SZN rushed for ninety-five yards on fifteen carries. The Starseekers had a dependable rushing contribution and a high-volume receiving option alongside the player who repeatedly finished the most valuable catches.
The defense supplied the first opening

Serp Gardener intercepted a short-middle Frosmoth pass at 4:18 of the first quarter and returned it twelve yards. Sunyshore converted the possession when Watzon found Arbok for a six-yard touchdown on third-and-four at 2:23. The missed extra point left the score 6–0. Hearthome then answered with Growlithe's fifty-four-yard field goal, keeping the margin at three through the end of the period.

That first quarter offers a useful check on the final score. The Haunts had made a costly mistake, yet they remained close enough for an ordinary scoring drive to change the lead. Sunyshore's subsequent performance created the rout. The opening minutes did not make it inevitable.

Watzon found Vick for an eight-yard touchdown with 4:20 left in the second quarter. After the extra point, Sunyshore led 13–3. Hearthome's next possession ended when Wugtrio fumbled following a six-yard run and @mped UP recovered. Swalot later scored from four yards out, giving the Starseekers a 20–3 advantage after the kick.

The defense had now supplied two possessions through takeaways, and Sunyshore had converted both into touchdowns. That is the specific standard the team established before halftime: create the opening, then finish it. The next quarter repeated the process more quickly and with much less opportunity for Hearthome to recover between errors.
The third-quarter sequence

body.alt: Five footballs on the Hearthome sideline symbolize Sunyshore’s five takeaways.
body.caption: Three interceptions and two recovered fumbles supplied Sunyshore with five extra possessions.

body.text: LaGatr caught a six-yard touchdown pass at 5:30 of the third. His broader contribution was sustained receiving work: ten catches on thirteen targets, with a longest gain of twenty. He gave Watzon repeated completions without needing a single enormous play to account for most of his yardage. The touchdown completed another useful possession and pushed the lead further out.

Gardener made his second interception at 3:30, taking a deep-left Frosmoth pass and returning it nineteen yards. Watzon immediately found Vick deep middle for a forty-two-yard touchdown. The pass began at 3:23. Sunyshore had moved from a takeaway to six points in one offensive play.

Hearthome then fumbled on its next offensive snap. Frosmoth completed an eleven-yard pass to Haunter at 3:14, but the receiver lost the ball and @mped UP recovered again. On third-and-nine at 2:49, Watzon found Vick on a short-right pass that became a thirty-five-yard touchdown. The receiver had scored twice in thirty-four seconds of game-clock time, with a defensive recovery between the two catches.

Vig Rothington intercepted another Frosmoth pass at 2:02 and returned it twenty-one yards. Sunyshore converted that possession too, this time on fourth-and-two. Watzon found EKTRIK RED for a four-yard touchdown at 0:46. The extra point made it 47–3. The Starseekers had scored four touchdowns in the quarter, three following takeaways.

Those sequences support the claim of defensive impact without requiring a guess about a hidden call or assignment. Gardener intercepted two passes. Rothington intercepted one. @mped UP recovered two fumbles. The recorded order shows Sunyshore's offense repeatedly taking advantage immediately afterward. Karson Jones received production from both units in a form that compounded within the same quarter.
Seven passing scores with several recipients

Vick's three touchdown receptions accounted for seventy-nine of his eighty-nine receiving yards. His other catch gained ten. LaGatr supplied the higher catch total, while Arbok, EKTRIK RED and MF STOMP each caught a touchdown. Watzon's seven scores therefore reached five different receivers. The passing game was concentrated enough to identify its principal finishers and broad enough that Hearthome could not limit the damage by surviving one matchup.

The rushing offense also deserves its place in that account. FLOAT SZN averaged 6.3 yards across fifteen carries, with a longest run of eleven. That is repeated useful production rather than one breakaway distorting the total. BAXXED? added nine yards, Vick seven and Swalot four, with the last contribution becoming the team's only rushing touchdown.

Watzon's protection allowed him to finish the day without a sack. Hearthome did record pressures, but none became a sack in the final passing line. The distinction matters: a quarterback can be hurried and still complete the play. Sunyshore's seven touchdown passes were the most important completed outcomes, especially when the defense had already reduced the amount of field the offense needed to cover.
Hearthome scored after the game had changed

The Haunts added fourteen fourth-quarter points. Frosmoth found Slowpoke for a nine-yard touchdown at 5:23 and Luvdisc for a fourteen-yard score at 1:38. Between them, Watzon hit MF STOMP for an eleven-yard touchdown. Those late scores improved Hearthome's final total without putting the result in doubt.

body.alt: Seven footballs in flight symbolize DeZhaun Watzon’s seven touchdown passes.
body.caption: Watzon’s seven passing scores helped the Starseekers finish a 53–17 win.

body.text: Frosmoth finished twenty-two of thirty-seven for 268 yards, two touchdowns and three interceptions. Haunter caught four passes for eighty-five yards; Wugtrio added sixty on four, and Abomasnow forty-six on four. Feraligatr rushed for fifty-one yards on nine carries. The offense did move the ball. Its five giveaways repeatedly prevented that movement from becoming a competitive score.

Sunyshore's defense added three sacks, one each from Torten Carter, Fred Whirler and BAXXED?. Gardener and Rothington supplied the interceptions, while Pat Serptain, 88 Special and Vick each recorded a forced fumble in the box score. A forced fumble is not automatically a recovered turnover, so the team's two recoveries remain the appropriate total when accounting for possessions.
Voices after the game

“That third quarter felt like somebody kept putting fresh batteries in the scoreboard,” Watzon said. “The defense would come back with the ball, and we would go back out.” The quarterback’s unusual description fitted the pace: repeated takeaways and quick touchdown throws kept adding points before Hearthome could establish a stable possession.

Vick was more exact about his own afternoon. “The throws gave me a chance to finish,” he said. “Four catches is a small number of plays. You have to make those plays count.” Three touchdowns from those four catches made his point efficiently. His forty-two-yard score immediately after Gardener’s second interception was the clearest example.

Karson Jones credited the connection between the two units. “Getting the ball back mattered. Scoring after we got it back mattered just as much,” he said. Canalave now presents a different task. Sunyshore can expect its next opponent to value possession after a low-scoring loss, and the Starseekers will need sustained execution if the opportunities arrive less frequently than they did in the third quarter at Hearthome.
Canalave arrives with a different approach

Sunyshore hosts Canalave next. The Bulwark are 7–5 after losing 14–6 at Eterna and have built their season around keeping scores manageable. Jones's team should expect a different assignment from the fast sequence of takeaways at Hearthome. The Starseekers can prepare to finish opportunities without assuming the opponent will supply five extra possessions.

The current injury report lists Myles Gabite with a zero-week medium entry. That is a reported status, not a guarantee about his next role. Sunyshore otherwise has the recent evidence of a productive available group: FLOAT SZN's rushing, LaGatr's repeated catches and Vick's scoring work all contributed to this win.

Hearthome, now 3–8–1, hosts Snowpoint after the Blizzard's overtime victory at Oreburgh. Fantina's team has enough recorded production to identify workable offensive pieces. The immediate correction is retaining the ball long enough for those pieces to matter. Sunyshore demonstrated the cost of failing to do so three times in a single quarter, then left with a division lead and seven touchdown passes to carry into the next week.

art.alt: DeZhaun Watzon, a Porygon-Z in Sunyshore number 30, throws a pass.

articles.title: Lavender wins again, then counts its available runners
articles.dek: Frosmoth threw two touchdowns in a 23–14 win over Mahogany, but Hobbes joins an already crowded injury report.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Lavender won a third consecutive game and received another reason to revisit its offensive personnel. The Wails beat Mahogany 23–14 behind Frosmoth's two touchdown passes and three Maractus field goals. Hobbes is now listed out two weeks. Mr. Clanky remains out one, and People Eater four. Travis Scarboro has built a winning run while the list of available answers keeps changing.

The victory moved Lavender to 7–5 and kept it in the current Kanto–Johto playoff field. Frosmoth completed eighteen of thirty-two for 219 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Wailord caught eight passes for ninety-seven yards and a score; Luvdisc caught seven for eighty. Samurott's only reception went thirty-three yards for the other passing touchdown.

Mahogany fell to 3–8–1. Porygon-Z threw two touchdowns without an interception, but completed eleven of twenty-three for 133 yards. Exploud gained forty-six rushing yards on fifteen carries. The Frost kept themselves within a score during the fourth quarter and still could not finish with the result their late opportunity required.
Two fumbles made the afternoon harder

The first quarter ended scoreless. Early in the second, Frosmoth completed a five-yard pass to Luvdisc, who fumbled. Lopunny recovered for Mahogany at 5:27. The Frost converted the opportunity when Porygon-Z found Golduck for a twenty-one-yard touchdown at 4:04. Lavender had supplied both a short completion and the possession that allowed the visitor to take the lead.

Frosmoth answered with the game's longest scoring pass. He found Samurott deep right for thirty-three yards at 1:56, tying the game after the extra point. Maractus added a twenty-two-yard field goal with five seconds left in the half, giving the Wails a 10–7 lead. Lavender had recovered from its turnover without requiring Mahogany to return the favor.

That is an important feature of the result. The Wails did not intercept Porygon-Z, and their own passing line also contained no interceptions. The decisive mistakes were fumbles after completed passes. Luvdisc's seven catches and eighty yards made him a major contributor, but his two lost possessions gave Mahogany chances to keep the game close.

The second came in the fourth quarter. With Lavender ahead 20–7, Frosmoth found Luvdisc for nineteen yards at 4:41. The receiver fumbled, and Watchog recovered for Mahogany. Porygon-Z then hit Lileep for a fourteen-yard touchdown at 3:54. The extra point brought the Frost within six. An afternoon that Lavender had worked to control again required a response.
The kicks preserved the useful margins

body.alt: Kujira, a Wailord in Lavender number 99, secures an American football.
body.caption: Kujira caught eight passes for ninety-seven yards and a touchdown.

body.text: Maractus made three field goals: twenty-two yards just before halftime, fifty-one at 4:46 of the third and thirty-seven at 1:54 of the fourth. The last was particularly consequential. It moved Lavender from a six-point lead to a nine-point lead after Mahogany had used the second fumble to score. The Frost then needed more than one ordinary touchdown possession to catch up.

The fifty-one-yard kick also matters in the sequence. Lavender entered the second half ahead by three and extended the margin to six before its next touchdown. Each successful kick increased the value of the defense's following stop. A three-field-goal afternoon can disappear behind the touchdown highlights; here the final margin was nine, and the last kick changed the requirements of Mahogany's comeback.

Wailord supplied Lavender's fourth-quarter touchdown on a seven-yard pass at 5:21. His eight catches on thirteen targets made him Frosmoth's most productive receiver. A longest reception of twenty-five helped him reach ninety-seven yards without requiring one spectacular play to carry the total. He provided repeated completions and then finished a scoring opportunity when the offense needed a larger margin.

Samurott's role was entirely different and equally clear in the record. One target, one catch, thirty-three yards and a touchdown. That single reception answered Mahogany's opening score. Lavender's two principal receiving totals explain how the offense sustained itself; Samurott's contribution explains how it converted one particular chance into seven points.
The running work was already shared

Machoke led Lavender with eleven carries for forty-five yards. Diggersby added thirty-seven on eight, and Hobbes gained sixteen on three. The distribution is useful when assessing the new injury report because the Wails already used more than one runner in this game. It provides evidence of actual alternatives, while leaving the next week's ordering and workload for the team to determine.

Hobbes had rushed for 118 yards in the previous week's 18–17 victory at Cianwood. His sixteen here came before the new two-week absence appeared on the report. The difference should not be turned into an invented account of when the injury occurred. The archived game does not establish an injury timestamp, and the final designation is the reliable statement of his current availability.

Machoke also has a minor entry with zero weeks reported. That differs from Hobbes's two-week absence. A zero-week counter alone does not establish the next starting assignment or the exact workload a player will receive. Lavender can identify Machoke and Diggersby as runners who contributed against Mahogany; it should continue to confirm the available group as the Azalea game approaches.

The same discipline applies at quarterback. Frosmoth's eighteen completions and two touchdowns are observed production. Mr. Clanky's one-week absence remains on the current report. Scarboro has reason to trust the replacement's recent work without announcing a permanent change or assuming a return date that has not yet been confirmed.
Mahogany found scores, then needed another

Golduck caught all three of his targets for forty-six yards and the opening touchdown. Audino also caught three of three, gaining seventeen. Sandy Shocks added eighteen receiving yards on one catch and seventeen on one run. Those contributions gave Porygon-Z several ways to move the offense, but the final passing total remained 133 yards.

body.alt: Lavender’s Frosmoth watches the field from the sideline.
body.caption: Frosmoth’s two touchdown passes helped Lavender reach 7–5.

body.text: Exploud's fifteen carries produced 3.1 yards per attempt, with a longest gain of ten. Lavender limited the back well enough that Mahogany could not simply repeat the rushing volume from its previous game. The Frost had gained 150 rushing yards in their one-point loss at Azalea; Exploud had accounted for eighty-four. This week, the available gains were smaller and the final result was another defeat.

Mahogany's two recovered fumbles were genuine opportunities. The offense turned both into touchdowns, so the problem was not wasting those particular possessions. It was failing to add enough around them. Lavender scored through two passing touchdowns and three field goals, while the Frost's points came entirely from the two scoring passes and their extra points.
Voices after the game

“We got the win. I want the next drive cleaner,” Frosmoth said. The quarterback’s impatience was understandable after a game that provided both productive passing and stretches when Lavender could have made the score more comfortable. His next opponent arrives before the Wails can assume their backfield is fully restored.

Wailord wanted the same quick move toward improvement. “Keep the good catches, fix the empty trips, get ready for Azalea,” he said. There was little interest in stretching a useful victory into a weeklong celebration. Lavender has moved into a position where its next result can matter directly to the shape of the wild-card chase.

Travis Scarboro kept his attention on the available personnel. “We prepare with the players who can go, and we give them jobs they can finish,” he said. The injury list makes that a practical concern. A recovery counter can describe progress without supplying a healthy runner for the next snap. Lavender’s preparation must account for the continuing absences while building on the passing contributions that helped settle this game.
Azalea is the next direct race game

Lavender hosts Azalea next. The Swarm are 5–7 and coming off a bye, with their most recent result an 18–17 win over Mahogany. The Wails can therefore compare two recent games against the same opponent without pretending the comparison settles the matchup. Both teams beat the Frost; Lavender did so with a different quarterback situation and now faces another change at running back.

The playoff context makes the next game particularly useful. Lavender is currently sixth in the conference, ahead of the clubs chasing the final places, while Azalea remains outside the seven. A win would strengthen the Wails' position and directly hurt a pursuer. A loss would give that pursuer a result against a team it is trying to catch. Those stakes are substantial without requiring an unsupported claim that either team can settle its whole season in one afternoon.

Mahogany hosts Mt. Silver next, immediately after the Reds secured Johto West with a 45–0 win. Pryce's team will need more production beyond the possessions its defense creates. Lavender, meanwhile, has three consecutive wins after four consecutive losses. Scarboro's next preparation begins with the players who produced this one and a fresh check of which of them can take the field against Azalea.

art.alt: Lavender’s Frosmoth, number 15, releases a pass.

articles.title: Rustboro answers the opener and stops the slide
articles.dek: Two first-half touchdowns and three takeaways carried the Stone past Mauville, 17–3, after a 23–0 defeat in their first meeting.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Rustboro found a much better way to spend an afternoon against Mauville. The Stone won 17–3, reversing the direction of a season series that began with a 23–0 defeat. Three takeaways helped keep the Dynamos out of the end zone, while two second-quarter touchdowns gave Rustboro enough offense to improve to 7–5.

Tyler Scarboro's team had just lost 35–7 to Mossdeep. Mauville arrived with consecutive wins and an earlier shutout against this opponent. Rustboro therefore had two recent reasons to expect a difficult game and one useful response: keep the visitor's scoring opportunities small enough that a modest offensive total would hold up.

Porygon-Z completed eighteen of twenty-seven for 236 yards without an interception. Lombre completed both of his passes for sixteen yards and the team's only passing touchdown. Gibby Timmy caught four passes for eighty-nine yards and that score. Philly rushed nine times for fifty-two yards, while Porygon-Z supplied the other touchdown on a one-yard run.
The first turnover arrived before the first points

Neither team scored in the first quarter. Mauville lost a possession when Bibarel fumbled after a seven-yard run at 1:22. Kricketune recovered for Rustboro. That gave the Stone an opportunity before either offense had established a scoring rhythm, and the home team eventually took the lead early in the second.

Lombre found Gibby Timmy for a nine-yard touchdown at 5:01. The Archeops caught the short-left throw. The useful detail is the change of passer: Porygon-Z produced most of Rustboro's passing yards, while Lombre delivered the scoring throw. The box score supports that division of work without requiring an invented explanation of the substitution.

Mauville answered with Sunflora's thirty-four-yard field goal at 2:33, a kick recorded as good off the upright. That was the visitor's only scoring play. The Dynamos still had time to build on it, but Rustboro added another touchdown before halftime. Porygon-Z ran up the middle from a yard out at 1:17, and the extra point made it 14–3.

The Stone had converted a scoreless opening period into an eleven-point halftime lead. The margin was useful rather than overwhelming. Mauville had enough passing production to remain a threat, and Rustboro still needed its defense to prevent one successful possession from turning the game back into a one-score contest.
Passing yards did not become Mauville touchdowns

body.alt: Rustboro’s Porygon-Z, number 37, carries the ball over the goal line.
body.caption: Porygon-Z added a one-yard rushing touchdown to his passing contribution.

body.text: Togekiss completed twenty-one of thirty-two for 239 yards, with no touchdown passes and two interceptions. Wigglytuff's only attempt was incomplete. Mauville's top receiving lines were productive: Mothim caught nine of ten targets for seventy-seven yards, Arbok added sixty-four on three catches and Tangrowth fifty-nine on four. Those totals show why the final three points require explanation beyond a claim that the Dynamos could not complete a pass.

Mothim repeatedly supplied catches, and Arbok had a forty-six-yard gain. Mauville nevertheless finished without a touchdown. The turnover on the ground removed one possession early, and two interceptions ended opportunities in the fourth quarter. Rustboro needed to defend the valuable parts of the field and retain enough possessions to protect its lead; it did both well enough to prevent the receiving totals from changing the result.

The rushing contribution was smaller. Bibarel gained thirty-one yards on seven carries, while Aipom lost a yard on his only attempt. Mauville finished with thirty rushing yards. That left much of the offensive responsibility with Togekiss and the receivers, and the two late interceptions became especially expensive when the ground game had supplied so little alternative production.

The Dynamos had gained useful momentum from consecutive wins before this trip. Their quarterback's yardage here shows that the passing game did not disappear completely. Wattson's review can be more specific: preserve the productive completions, improve the finishing, and stop giving the defense another possession at the moments when the deficit is still manageable.
Two interceptions closed the fourth quarter

The third quarter produced no points. Rustboro's eleven-point lead survived, but the offense did not extend it. That left the fourth quarter with a clear task for both teams: Mauville needed a touchdown to make the game urgent, while the Stone needed either another score or a turnover that prevented that pressure from arriving.

Huntail supplied the first interception at 4:58, taking a Togekiss deep-right pass and returning it thirteen yards. Gorebyss then made a forty-two-yard field goal at 3:47. The lead became 17–3. Rustboro had turned a defensive takeaway into the additional points that Mauville's offense was trying to find for itself.

Frosmoth made the second interception at 1:50, collecting a deep-left pass and returning it ten yards. The Stone had now taken the ball three times across the game: Kricketune's fumble recovery and the two fourth-quarter interceptions. Those are the possessions that distinguish the defensive performance from the raw yardage comparison.

Porygon-Z and Lombre combined for 252 passing yards, thirteen more than Mauville's total. Neither threw an interception. Rustboro's passing advantage was therefore small in yards and much larger in retained opportunities. The home team did not need to win every statistical comparison by a wide margin to win the scoreboard by fourteen.
Timmy led a useful receiving spread

Gibby Timmy's eighty-nine yards included a thirty-seven-yard reception and the nine-yard touchdown. Gengar caught all three of his targets for sixty yards, with a longest gain of forty-three. Shieldon caught five of six for fifty-three. Rustboro received important work from several targets rather than relying exclusively on the scorer to move the offense.

That spread is particularly welcome with My Way, Son still listed out five weeks. The absence remains substantial, and this game does not make it disappear. It does provide a concrete account of which available receivers supplied production against Mauville. Timmy led in yards, Shieldon led those three in receptions and Gengar supplied the longest catch among them.

body.alt: Rustboro’s Lombre, number 31, throws a pass.
body.caption: Lombre supplied Rustboro’s touchdown pass on a nine-yard throw to Gibby Timmy.

body.text: Philly's fifty-two rushing yards came at 5.8 per carry, with a longest run of nineteen. Watchog added sixteen on five attempts. Porygon-Z's five carries produced only three net yards but included the one-yard touchdown. As in several games around the league this week, a modest quarterback rushing total still contained a valuable scoring finish.

The current report lists Porygon-Z with a minor injury entry carrying zero weeks. That should remain a reported status, separate from any claim about the next week's workload. His completed passes and rushing touchdown are established facts from the Mauville game. Rustboro can use those facts to assess the offense while continuing to check availability before its next trip.
Voices after the game

“Three points was a generous opening gift,” Timmy said. “We decided the visitors had received enough.” The Archeops could afford the joke after Rustboro answered Mauville’s early field goal and controlled the scoring afterward. His touchdown was part of a response that gave the home crowd a reason to enjoy the evening again.

Timmy’s touchdown also belonged to Lombre, whose two completions supplied sixteen yards and the scoring throw. Porygon-Z handled most of the passing work and added the rushing touchdown. Rustboro had productive contributions from both passers, and its defense ensured the seventeen points were sufficient.

Tyler Scarboro described the win as useful preparation for Fortree. “We answered their first score and kept playing the game in front of us,” he said. “That is what we need again.” Fortree will arrive in the next meeting carrying a much heavier defeat, but Rustboro’s own recent losses should discourage any assumption that the opponent’s last score settles the next contest. The Stone have regained momentum and still have a crowded race to navigate.
Fortree is next, and the race stays close

The Stone visit Fortree in Week 14. The Skyhawks just allowed seventy-nine points to Mossdeep, but Rustboro has its own recent evidence of how quickly a previous score can become an unreliable forecast. Mauville won the first meeting 23–0; Rustboro won this one 17–3. Scarboro can prepare for Fortree's actual players and recent mistakes without treating another team's margin as a promised outcome.

Rustboro currently holds the fifth Hoenn–Sinnoh seed at 7–5, level in record with Canalave and Dewford. Petalburg leads Hoenn West at 9–3 and visits Mossdeep next. The Stone therefore have an immediate chance to improve their own position while the division leader faces the league's unbeaten team. That is a useful schedule circumstance, with the result at Fortree still required before any benefit can be counted.

Mauville, now 5–7, travels to Lavaridge after losing ground in the wild-card chase. The Dynamos can point to twenty-one completions and several productive receivers. Rustboro can point to two touchdowns, three takeaways and a fourth quarter in which it added points while taking away the visitor's remaining chances. Those are the improvements that turned the rematch into the Stone's seventh win.

art.alt: Gibby Timmy, an Archeops in Rustboro number 99, lands near the sideline.
